section.title: Amnon and Tamar
section.sectionRationale: The consequences Nathan announced begin to fall inside David's own house. His son Amnon, aided by a shrewd cousin, lures and rapes his half-sister Tamar, then throws her out in cold hatred. David is furious but does nothing, and Tamar is left desolate. Two years later Absalom, her brother, takes revenge by murdering Amnon at a feast and flees into exile. The movement is a harrowing account of lust, violence, injustice, and vengeance, the sword rising within David's family exactly as the LORD had warned.
section.thesis: The sword promised to David's house begins its work through his own children: Amnon's lust becomes rape and then hatred, David's failure to act leaves evil unpunished and a victim desolate, and Absalom's smoldering revenge becomes murder, showing how sin unaddressed festers into deeper ruin across a family.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Amnon's scheme and the rape of Tamar, verses 1 to 19; the desolation of Tamar and David's inaction, verses 20 to 22; and Absalom's revenge on Amnon and flight to Geshur, verses 23 to 39.

units.label: Amnon's crime against Tamar
units.note: such a thing should never be done in Israel

verses.text: After some time, David’s son Amnon fell in love with Tamar, the beautiful sister of David’s son Absalom.
Amnon was sick with frustration over his sister Tamar, for she was a virgin, and it seemed implausible for him to do anything to her.
Now Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very shrewd man,
and he asked Amnon, “Why are you, the son of the king, so depressed morning after morning? Won’t you tell me?” Amnon replied, “I am in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom’s sister.”

Jonadab told him, “Lie down on your bed and pretend you are ill. When your father comes to see you, say to him, ‘Please let my sister Tamar come and give me something to eat. Let her prepare it in my sight so I may watch her and eat it from her hand.’”
So Amnon lay down and feigned illness. When the king came to see him, Amnon said, “Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes in my sight, so that I may eat from her hand.”
Then David sent word to Tamar at the palace: “Please go to the house of Amnon your brother and prepare a meal for him.”
So Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down. She took some dough, kneaded it, made cakes in his sight, and baked them.
Then she brought the pan and set it down before him, but he refused to eat. “Send everyone away!” said Amnon. And everyone went out.
Then Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom, so that I may eat it from your hand.” Tamar took the cakes she had made and went to her brother Amnon’s bedroom.
And when she had brought them to him to eat, he took hold of her and said, “Come lie with me, my sister!”
“No, my brother!” she cried. “Do not violate me, for such a thing should never be done in Israel. Do not do this {{nebalah|disgraceful thing}}!
Where could I ever take my shame? And you would be like one of the fools in Israel! Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you.”
But Amnon refused to listen to her, and being stronger, he violated her and lay with her.
Then Amnon {{sane|hated}} Tamar with such intensity that his hatred was greater than the love he previously had. “Get up!” he said to her. “Be gone!”
“No,” she replied, “sending me away is worse than this great wrong you have already done to me!” But he refused to listen to her.
Instead, he called to his attendant and said, “Throw this woman out and bolt the door behind her!”
So Amnon’s attendant threw her out and bolted the door behind her. Now Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors, because this is what the king’s virgin daughters wore.
And Tamar put ashes on her head and tore her robe. And putting her hand on her head, she went away crying aloud.

units.label: Tamar desolate, David silent
units.note: the king was furious but did nothing

verses.text: Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? Be quiet for now, my sister. He is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart.” So Tamar lived as a desolate woman in the house of her brother Absalom.
When King David heard all this, he was furious.
And Absalom never said a word to Amnon, either good or bad, because he hated Amnon for violating his sister Tamar.

units.label: Absalom's revenge
units.note: the sword rises in David's house

verses.text: Two years later, when Absalom’s sheepshearers were at Baal-hazor near Ephraim, he invited all the sons of the king.
And he went to the king and said, “Your servant has just hired shearers. Will the king and his servants please come with me?”
“No, my son,” the king replied, “we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” Although Absalom urged him, he was not willing to go, but gave him his blessing.
“If not,” said Absalom, “please let my brother Amnon go with us.” “Why should he go with you?” the king asked.
But Absalom urged him, so the king sent Amnon and the rest of his sons.

Now Absalom had ordered his young men, “Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine, and when I order you to strike Amnon down, you are to kill him. Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and valiant!”
So Absalom’s young men did to Amnon just as Absalom had ordered. Then all the other sons of the king got up, and each one fled on his mule.
While they were on the way, a report reached David: “Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!”
Then the king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground. And all his servants stood by with their clothes torn.

But Jonadab, the son of David’s brother Shimeah, spoke up: “My lord must not think they have killed all the sons of the king, for only Amnon is dead. In fact, Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.
So now, my lord the king, do not take to heart the report that all the sons of the king are dead. Only Amnon is dead.”

Meanwhile, Absalom had fled. When the young man standing watch looked up, he saw many people coming down the road west of him, along the side of the hill. And the watchman went and reported to the king, “I see men coming from the direction of Horonaim, along the side of the hill.”
So Jonadab said to the king, “Look, the sons of the king have arrived! It is just as your servant said.”
And as he finished speaking, the sons of the king came in, wailing loudly. Then the king and all his servants also wept very bitterly.
Now Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, the king of Geshur. But David mourned for his son every day.
After Absalom had fled and gone to Geshur, he stayed there three years.
And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death.

nebalah.gloss: A disgraceful outrage, senseless folly, a wicked act that violates the moral order of God's people. Tamar names Amnon's intended act a nebalah, 'such a thing should never be done in Israel,' the same grave word used for the worst crimes in the law. It marks the deed not as a private wrong but as an assault on the covenant community's most sacred bonds.

sane.gloss: To hate, to reject with hostility. What Amnon called love was only lust, and once his desire is spent he sane, hated Tamar, with a hatred greater than his supposed love. The word exposes the difference between selfish craving and true love: craving discards its object, while love seeks the good of the other. Amnon's hatred adds cruelty to violence, casting Tamar out to compound her ruin.

basic.context: Nathan had told David that because of his sin the sword would never leave his house and that evil would rise against him from his own family. Chapter 13 shows the first terrible installment. David's oldest son Amnon becomes obsessed with his beautiful half-sister Tamar. His cunning cousin Jonadab devises a scheme: Amnon feigns illness and asks that Tamar come and cook for him. David, unwittingly, sends her. Alone with her, Amnon seizes Tamar. She pleads with him not to commit such a disgraceful outrage, offering any other path, but he overpowers and rapes her. Then, in a chilling turn, his lust curdles into hatred, and he has her thrown out and the door bolted. Tamar tears the royal robe of the virgin princesses, puts ashes on her head, and is left a desolate woman in her brother Absalom's house. David hears and is furious but, tellingly, does nothing to punish Amnon or restore Tamar. Absalom says nothing to Amnon but nurses his hatred for two years, then lures Amnon to a sheepshearing feast and has him murdered, before fleeing into exile at Geshur. The chapter raises hard questions about lust masquerading as love, the failure of a father to do justice, the desolation of a victim, and the ruin that spreads when sin is neither confronted nor healed.
basic.hermeneutics: This is unflinching historical narrative, description of grievous evil, never its endorsement. Tamar is portrayed with dignity and given a voice; the text clearly condemns Amnon's crime as a disgraceful outrage and exposes his hatred and cruelty. David's inaction is reported as a failure, an ancient manuscript tradition even noting he would not punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn. The chapter must not be read as blaming Tamar; the guilt is entirely Amnon's, and later Absalom's for his murder. The passage teaches by showing the bitter fruit of unrestrained lust, injustice, and vengeance within a family under God's announced discipline.
basic.originalLanguages: Tamar names the intended crime with the gravest word available, nebalah, a disgraceful outrage, 'such a thing should never be done in Israel,' the term the law reserves for acts that tear the fabric of God's people. And the narrator exposes the lie beneath Amnon's so-called love with a single verb: once his desire is satisfied he sane, hated Tamar, more than he had ever 'loved' her. Together the words tell the truth of the scene, a wicked outrage driven not by love but by lust that, spent, turns to hatred and cruelty.
basic.typology: This chapter offers no positive type but a dark negative one: the sons of David here are the opposite of the true Son of David. Amnon takes and defiles by force, then hates; the true Son of David gives Himself in love and never casts out the one who comes to Him. Tamar, the innocent sufferer left desolate and unavenged by an earthly king's inaction, cries out for a King who will do justice for the violated and the crushed, a longing answered only in Christ.
basic.christ: The horror of this chapter drives us to long for the true King. Where Amnon's craving used and discarded, Christ's love lays down His life for His bride and will never cast out the one who comes to Him. Where David failed to do justice for his violated daughter, Christ is the righteous Judge who sees every violation, defends the crushed, and will right every wrong. And where sin's sword ran through David's house because sin was covered rather than confronted, Christ deals with sin fully at the cross, breaking its power to spread and destroy.
basic.god: God is not named as acting in this chapter, and His silence is part of its horror, yet the whole scene unfolds under the discipline He had announced through Nathan, so that even this evil is within, not outside, His sovereign warning to David. God is the God who hears the cry of the desolate like Tamar, who hates the outrage that men commit, and who will not leave injustice unanswered forever. The chapter's darkness makes us long for the God who judges rightly and heals the broken.
basic.crossReferences: Second Samuel 12 gives Nathan's warning that the sword would not leave David's house and evil rise from within it, now being fulfilled. Genesis 34 uses the same word 'disgraceful thing' for the violation of Dinah. Leviticus 18 forbids the incest Amnon commits. And Christ's promise never to cast out the one who comes to Him, John 6, stands in stark contrast to Amnon casting out Tamar.
basic.oneStory: The sword the LORD warned of begins to fall within David's own family, as lust becomes rape, injustice leaves a victim desolate, and hatred becomes murder. This harrowing chapter exposes the ruin that sin spreads when it is neither confronted nor healed, and it makes us ache for the true Son of David, who does not defile but redeems, who does not cast out but welcomes, and who will do perfect justice for every Tamar the world has crushed.

context.literary:
The chapter runs two extended appeals back to back that both go unheeded, Tamar's plea in verses 12 and 13 and, later, David's simple refusal followed by Absalom's persistent urging in verses 24 to 27, and in both cases patient, reasoned speech is overridden by someone stronger or more insistent, first Amnon's lust, then Absalom's persuasion. That pairing quietly indicts both brothers with the same failure, refusing to let a reasonable word stand in the way of a fixed intention.

The chapter is also bracketed by two kinds of ruinous fixation. It opens with Amnon so obsessed with Tamar that he makes himself sick over her, verse 2, and closes with David so consumed with longing for the exiled Absalom that his grief for the murdered Amnon finally gives way to it, verse 39; misplaced desire opens the chapter and misplaced longing closes it, framing the whole tragedy as a family repeatedly ruled by feeling rather than by justice. In between, the two year silence of verse 23 mirrors the pattern already set by the previous two chapters, where sin and its reckoning are separated by a deliberate gap of time, long enough for the reader, like Absalom, to wonder whether anything will ever be done.
context.historical:
Tamar's desperate suggestion, please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you, verse 13, sits uneasily beside the law's clear prohibition of sexual relations between a man and his sister or half sister, Leviticus 18:9 and 11, and 20:17; whether she is grasping at any argument she can find in the moment of crisis, or dimly recalling an older patriarchal custom like Abraham's own marriage to his half sister Sarah, Genesis 20:12, which the law given at Sinai had since closed off, the text does not say, and either way her words are the plea of a woman searching for any way out, not a legal opinion to be weighed against Moses.

Sheepshearing was a festive, often heavy drinking occasion across the ancient Near East, the same setting in which Nabal is caught off guard by his own drunkenness in 1 Samuel 25, which made it exactly the kind of gathering where a planned ambush could hide behind ordinary celebration. That each of the king's sons flees on his own mule, verse 29, marks their standing as royalty, since mules were prized, elite mounts, the very animal Solomon later rides at his own coronation, 1 Kings 1:33. And Geshur, where Absalom flees, was his own mother Maacah's homeland, a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee, 2 Samuel 3:3, safely beyond David's reach and offering the one place a fugitive prince of Israel could expect real protection.
context.canonical:
This chapter stands at the head of the long narrative unit running through chapter 20, often called the succession narrative, which traces how David's failure to deal with sin in his own house unravels his family and nearly costs him his throne. Absalom's three years at Geshur, verse 38, is only the first stage of an exile that stretches further once his eventual return to Jerusalem is added, where he lives two more years without seeing the king's face, 2 Samuel 14:28, showing how far a single unpunished crime and a single act of silent grief can travel before the family is even partly reconciled, let alone healed.

The chapter also joins a recurring biblical pattern in which a father's failure to act opens the door to a son's excessive and unauthorized vengeance. Jacob says nothing decisive after Shechem violates Dinah, and his sons Simeon and Levi answer with a massacre that appalls even their father, Genesis 34:30; David is furious but does nothing after Amnon violates Tamar, and his son Absalom answers, two years later, with a calculated murder. Neither son's vengeance is commended by the narrator in either book, yet both stories place real responsibility on the father whose silence left the field open for it.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The narrator wants the reader to watch Nathan's word, the sword will never depart from your house, begin to come true inside David's own household, and he wants it to come true through entirely human, morally responsible choices rather than any direct divine intervention, so that the horror of the chapter is never allowed to become someone else's fault but the characters' own. He gives Tamar an unusually long, clear, and reasoned speech, verses 12 and 13, the fullest sustained resistance any woman voices in these books, precisely so that no reader can later claim she was complicit or unclear about what was happening to her.

He also means the reader to see how each failure compounds the next: Amnon's lust becomes assault, David's fury becomes only fury and nothing more, and Absalom's silence becomes two years of plotted revenge. None of these men learns from the others' failure; each simply adds his own, and the chapter's plain, unflinching reporting is itself the author's verdict, that a family's unaddressed sin does not stay contained to the person who first commits it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nothing here is prescriptive. The chapter reports a rape, a father's failure of justice, and a calculated murder without commending any of the three, and its silence about direct divine comment should not be read as divine indifference, only as the narrator's method of letting plain report carry its own verdict, as it did already two chapters earlier. What does transfer forward as abiding instruction is diagnostic rather than directive: lust disguises itself as love and then reveals itself in cruelty once satisfied, verse 15; a leader's failure to punish real wrongdoing does not preserve peace but only postpones and often worsens conflict, as Absalom's two years of silence show; and a victim's clear, articulate resistance, as Tamar gives here, deserves to be believed and acted upon rather than managed away with a brother's soft word, be quiet for now, verse 20.

debates.question: Why does David, though furious, do nothing to punish Amnon or restore Tamar?

views.label: A failure of justice rooted in David's compromised authority
views.case: David is furious but takes no action, and an ancient reading preserved in the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint adds that he would not punish Amnon because he loved him as his firstborn; David's own sin with Bathsheba had undercut his moral authority to judge his son's sexual crime, so his paralysis is best read as a real failure that leaves Tamar desolate and emboldens Absalom to take justice into his own hands.

views.label: Weak parental partiality with tragic results
views.case: Others emphasize David's pattern of indulgent, passive parenting seen across these chapters, failing to restrain or discipline his sons; whether from favoritism, guilt, or weakness, his inaction is a dereliction of the king's duty to do justice, and the narrative presents it as a cause of the deepening disaster, not as wise restraint.

debates.bearing: Either way the text presents David's inaction as a grievous failure, not a virtue; a victim is left without justice and a murderer is left unchecked, illustrating how a leader's compromised authority and passivity allow evil to spread, and heightening the longing for the righteous King who will judge justly and defend the crushed.

debates.question: How culpable is Jonadab, Amnon's shrewd cousin, in what follows?

views.label: A shrewd, self-serving enabler culpable for what follows
views.case: Jonadab's scheme directly manufactures the opportunity for the crime, verses 3 to 5, and his later precise, calm knowledge of Absalom's long-planned revenge, verses 32 and 33, suggests a man who reads every prince's intentions with unsettling accuracy yet serves whichever one currently needs his cleverness. The narrator's pointed description of him as very shrewd, verse 3, framing both the crime and its bloody aftermath, invites the reader to see intelligence used with no loyalty to what is right.

views.label: A bystander whose insight is unsettling but not proven complicity
views.case: The text never states that Jonadab knew in advance that Absalom would murder Amnon, only that he correctly reads the situation once news of the killing arrives; some readers hesitate to convict him of a foreknowledge the narrative does not explicitly claim, treating his shrewdness as merely disturbing rather than criminal.

debates.bearing: Whichever is closer to the truth, the narrator's repeated, pointed description of Jonadab as very shrewd invites the reader to notice how cleverness untethered from care for what is right can serve almost any harm in a family already primed for it, whether Jonadab is judged an active accomplice or merely an unsettling bystander.

study.originalLanguages:
A single Hebrew root ties this chapter back to chapter 10 in the darkest possible way. There, chazaq named Joab's call to courage, be strong and let us fight bravely for our people, 2 Samuel 10:12. Here the same root describes Amnon overpowering his sister, being stronger, he violated her and lay with her, verse 14; the word that once meant valor turned outward against real enemies is turned inward, against a defenseless member of David's own household, and the narrator's choice to use it here rather than a softer term for compulsion makes the assault, quite deliberately, an act of raw physical force rather than seduction.

The verb translated violate, used four times across this chapter, verses 12, 14, 22, and 32, is the same verb the law uses for a man who forces another man's wife, the man because he has violated his neighbor's wife, Deuteronomy 22:24, and for a man who seizes an unbetrothed woman, because he has violated her, Deuteronomy 22:29. Its fourfold repetition inside one chapter is not narrative padding but insistence, the text will not let the reader soften what happened into a lesser word, and the law's own use of it elsewhere shows Israel already had precise legal vocabulary for exactly this crime.

The chapter also plays a grim wordgame with sickness. Amnon is described in verse 2 as sick with frustration, and the same word for sick returns when Jonadab coaches him, pretend you are ill, verse 5, and when Amnon feigned illness, verse 6. A real inward sickness, unmastered desire, is dressed up as a physical illness to manipulate a father's compassion, so that the very word for Amnon's disordered heart becomes the costume he wears to get what that heart wants.

And the word nebalah, already named in the lexicon, deserves one further note here: it is the same term Israel's law and later writers reserve for acts that threaten the whole community's moral order, not merely private wrongs, rendered outrage when Shechem violates Dinah, a thing that should not be done, Genesis 34:7, when Achan breaks faith with what was devoted to destruction, committed an outrage in Israel, Joshua 7:15, and when the men of Gibeah threaten their guest, do not commit this outrage, Judges 19:23. Tamar names her coming violation with this same gravest word available to her, insisting from the very start that this is not a private family matter between siblings but an outrage against Israel itself, such a thing should never be done in Israel, verse 12, a claim the rest of the chapter, and the two years of silence that follow, tragically proves true rather than false.

typology.type: Tamar's long, reasoned resistance overridden by superior force, 2 Samuel 13:12-14.
typology.fulfillment: Tamar names the crime plainly, appeals to Israel's moral order, and even proposes a lawful alternative, yet reasoned resistance cannot stop a stronger will bent on having its way. Scripture elsewhere insists that the LORD is exactly the kind of judge who does hear such resistance and finally acts on it, will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night, Luke 18:7, so that Tamar's unanswered plea in this chapter becomes, for every reader who has cried out and not yet seen justice, a small dark mirror of the promise that God's ear is not likewise deaf.

typology.type: A brother's counsel to be quiet and not take it to heart, 2 Samuel 13:20.
typology.fulfillment: Absalom's well meant but damaging advice silences Tamar rather than pursuing justice for her, leaving grief with nowhere to go but inward, where it hardens into two years of hidden plotting. The contrast is sharp with the God who tells His suffering people to pour out their hearts before Him, trust in Him at all times, Psalm 62:8, refusing the false comfort of quiet suppression and instead inviting the wronged to bring their whole grief, unfiltered, into His presence rather than sit with it alone.

typology.type: A father furious yet unwilling to act, 2 Samuel 13:21.
typology.fulfillment: David's anger without consequence leaves both a victim unvindicated and a wrongdoer unchecked, a pattern that measures exactly what the true King refuses to do. God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil, Ecclesiastes 12:14, so that David's failure to follow feeling with action becomes the very thing the coming King, who both feels and acts, will finally put right.

typology.type: Two years of hidden hatred erupting into planned murder, 2 Samuel 13:23-29.
typology.fulfillment: Absalom's silence is not peace but a slow fuse, unaddressed injury curdling, exactly as it did once already in this family, into calculated violence rather than confessed grief. Paul's warning could have been written for this brother directly, do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold, Ephesians 4:26 to 27, naming in one line the very door Absalom's two years of silence quietly opened.

study.christ:
Every figure in this chapter fails in a way the true Son of David does not, and the failures are worth naming one by one rather than blurred together. Amnon takes what is not his and then despises the very person he claimed to love, hatred greater than the love he previously had, verse 15; Christ's love does the opposite of every direction desire can run, having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end, John 13:1, a love that does not cool once it has what it wants because it was never about getting something in the first place.

David, though furious, does nothing, leaving a wronged daughter without justice and a wrongdoer unchecked, verse 21; the true King does not merely feel the weight of injustice, He acts on it without fail, He will not grow weak or discouraged before He has established justice on the earth, Isaiah 42:4, a promise this chapter's silence makes the reader long for rather than assume. Absalom nurses a private hatred for two years until it becomes murder, verses 22 and 28 to 29; Christ, wronged infinitely more and with every right to answer violence with violence, instead entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23, breaking rather than continuing the family's pattern of injury answered with injury.

And Tamar herself, left desolate, unheard by her father, unavenged by anyone, most clearly anticipates the reversal only Christ secures. He does not merely feel for the wounded from a distance; He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, Isaiah 53:3, entering fully into the kind of desolation this chapter records rather than remaining untouched by it, and He promises that the one who comes to Him, whatever has been done to them, He will never cast out, John 6:37, the one line in all of Scripture that answers Amnon's bolted door with an open one.
study.god:
This chapter contains fewer words about God than almost any other passage in Samuel; the LORD is never quoted, never described as acting, never even mentioned by David or anyone else across thirty nine verses. That silence is not evidence of absence, since the whole scene unfolds precisely within the discipline the LORD had already announced through Nathan, the sword will never depart from your house, 2 Samuel 12:10, so that even here, when it looks as though only human beings are moving the story forward, the chapter's placement itself is a statement about God's ongoing governance of what David's sin has set in motion.

God's apparent silence in this chapter is itself a kind of theology, and a hard one: it teaches that His people sometimes suffer real evil without any recorded word of comfort or intervention in the moment itself, which is exactly the experience many who suffer abuse and injustice know firsthand, an absence of visible rescue that does not, elsewhere in Scripture, mean an absence of notice. The God who tells Cain that his brother's blood cries out to Him from the ground, Genesis 4:10, is not a God indifferent to unavenged violence, even when a chapter about it never quotes Him directly.

The hardest honesty this chapter forces onto its reader is that the LORD does not step in to stop Amnon, does not move David to justice, and does not restrain Absalom's plotting, allowing genuinely evil, human, chosen acts to run their course inside the family of His own anointed king. That restraint is not the same as approval; nothing in the surrounding narrative, or in the rest of Scripture's treatment of rape, murder, and injustice, suggests God delights in any of it. What this chapter's silence does is throw the reader forward, past David's failed justice and Absalom's private vengeance, toward the God who has promised that no hidden thing will remain hidden forever and that every cry unheard by an earthly father is still heard by Him.

crossReferences.note: Nathan's warning that the sword would never leave David's house and that evil would rise from within it is fulfilled precisely here, one chapter later, as David's own son commits the very kind of violence the prophet foretold. The prophecy is not vague foreboding but begins to be answered in exact, traceable detail.

The law forbidding sexual relations with a sister or half-sister, which Amnon violates, was already in force by this point in Israel's history, making his scheme a direct assault on a settled command rather than an ambiguous grey area his culture had not yet addressed.

Jacob's sons call Shechem's violation of their sister Dinah an outrage, a thing that should not be done, the same grave category of crime Tamar names for what Amnon intends. Both texts mark the assault as a wound to the whole community's order, not a private matter between two families.

Jesus tells the crowd that whoever comes to Him He will by no means turn away, an assurance aimed at anyone tempted to think a past wound or a past wrong makes them unwelcome. Read against the bolted door of verses 17 and 18, it answers Amnon's rejection of Tamar with a welcome that has no equivalent limit.

Jesus promises that God will bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night, and will not delay forever. Tamar's cry in this chapter finds no earthly answer, but the promise stands behind every unanswered cry like hers, that God's justice, though it may be slow by human reckoning, is not indefinitely withheld.

Paul's warning not to let the sun set on anger, and not to give the devil a foothold, describes exactly what Absalom does across two full years of concealed hatred, verses 22 and 23. His silence is not the absence of anger but anger given a very long foothold indeed.

The Servant is described as despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, language that gathers up every kind of desolation this chapter records in Tamar. Christ enters that same category of suffering rather than observing it from a distance.

Peter says that when Christ suffered abuse, He did not retaliate or make threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. Absalom's answer to real injury is two years of silence followed by murder; Christ's answer to far greater injury is entrusted, patient trust in a righteous Judge.

The law's own vocabulary for sexual assault, describing a man who has violated a woman by force, matches the word used four times in this chapter, showing Israel already possessed a precise legal category for exactly this crime rather than leaving it undefined or excusable.

The Preacher's conclusion, that God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil, answers the chapter's most troubling feature, a crime met with fury but no earthly justice. What David leaves unresolved, ultimate judgment does not leave unresolved.

David elsewhere counsels God's people to trust in Him at all times and pour out their hearts before Him, exactly what Absalom's advice to Tamar, be quiet for now, prevents her from doing openly. The psalm offers the honest lament this chapter's silencing denies her a voice for.

The LORD tells Cain that his murdered brother's blood cries out to Him from the ground, proof that unavenged violence is never actually unnoticed by God, even when, as in this chapter, no divine response is recorded at the time it happens.

study.oneStory:
This chapter is the moment the sword Nathan promised begins visibly cutting, and it belongs to the long biblical story of how one generation's unaddressed sin becomes the next generation's active wound. David's adultery and murder are answered, one chapter later, by his own son's rape of his own daughter, and the parallels are exact and deliberate, a king who saw and took becomes a son who saw and took, a father's private sin becomes a son's public crime, so that the whole scene reads as sin's inheritance rather than an isolated new tragedy.

The chapter also belongs to the Bible's wider testimony about victims whose cry seems to go unanswered for a long time. Tamar's desolation, verse 20, joins Joseph's pit, the Israelites' groaning under Egypt, and countless psalms of lament that ask how long before anyone will act, a category of suffering Scripture never rushes past or explains away, and never pretends is quickly resolved. The two years of silence before Absalom's revenge, and the further years of exile and estrangement that follow, show how long injustice can be left to fester once a father, or a whole family, decides that furious feeling is an adequate substitute for actual justice.

Yet the chapter's darkness is not the end of this family's story or of the Bible's larger one. The sword that begins here in Amnon's death will run through Absalom's own revolt and death before God graciously brings Solomon, born earlier of this same troubled union, to the throne in peace. And the whole ugly pattern, desire twisted into violence, silence mistaken for peace, revenge mistaken for justice, is finally answered not by another human king repeating the cycle but by the true Son of David, who breaks it, absorbing violence rather than multiplying it and promising a day when every Tamar's cry will be heard and answered in full.

quiz.q: How does Amnon commit his crime against Tamar?

options.text: He feigns illness on Jonadab's advice, gets Tamar sent to cook for him, then overpowers and rapes her despite her pleas.
options.note: Verses 5-14 record the scheme and the assault against Tamar's clear protest.

options.text: He openly asks David for Tamar's hand and is refused, then takes her by force.
options.note: Amnon does not seek marriage openly; he schemes with Jonadab to get Tamar alone and assaults her.

options.text: He lures Tamar to his house under a false pretext and violates her.
options.note: True, but this option omits the role of Jonadab's scheme and David's unwitting part in sending Tamar.

options.text: He is seduced by Tamar and gives in to temptation.
options.note: The text places all guilt on Amnon; Tamar pleads against the crime and is the victim, not a seducer.

quiz.q: What does Amnon's treatment of Tamar after the assault reveal?

options.text: That his 'love' was only lust, for once his desire was spent he hated her and cruelly cast her out.
options.note: Verse 15 exposes his hatred, greater than his supposed love, and his cruelty in expelling her.

options.text: That he genuinely loved her but was ashamed of what he had done.
options.note: The text says he hated her intensely, the opposite of love or godly shame.

options.text: That his desire turned to hatred once it was satisfied.
options.note: True, but this option omits the added cruelty of throwing Tamar out and bolting the door against her.

options.text: That he immediately regretted his sin and sought to make it right.
options.note: He shows no repentance; he compounds the wrong by casting Tamar out to deepen her ruin.

quiz.q: How does David respond when he hears what Amnon did?

options.text: He is furious but does nothing to punish Amnon or restore Tamar, a failure of justice.
options.note: Verse 21 shows David's anger without action, leaving the crime unaddressed.

options.text: He immediately puts Amnon on trial and has him punished.
options.note: The opposite; David takes no action against Amnon at all.

options.text: He is angry but fails to act, leaving the wrong unaddressed.
options.note: True, but this option omits that a victim was left desolate and a murderer, Absalom, was thereby emboldened.

options.text: He comforts Tamar personally and restores her honor.
options.note: David does not restore Tamar; she is left desolate in Absalom's house while David does nothing.

quiz.q: How does Absalom respond to the outrage against his sister?

options.text: He says nothing to Amnon for two years, then lures him to a feast, has him murdered, and flees into exile.
options.note: Verses 22-38 record Absalom's patient, cold revenge and flight to Geshur.

options.text: He forgives Amnon and seeks reconciliation within the family.
options.note: The opposite; Absalom nurses hatred and eventually kills Amnon.

options.text: He takes revenge by having Amnon killed at a feast.
options.note: True, but this option omits the chilling two-year silence in which his hatred was concealed and premeditated.

options.text: He appeals to David to bring Amnon to justice through the courts.
options.note: Absalom does not appeal to David; he takes vengeance into his own hands.

quiz.q: How does this dark chapter point us toward Christ?

options.text: By contrast: where these sons of David defile, cast out, and fail to do justice, the true Son of David loves, welcomes, and judges rightly for the crushed.
options.note: The chapter's evils make us long for Christ, John 6:37 and Luke 18:7-8.

options.text: By showing that God's people should take revenge into their own hands as Absalom did.
options.note: The chapter condemns the whole chain of sin, including Absalom's murder; it does not commend vengeance.

options.text: By making us long for a King who will do justice for the violated and never cast them out.
options.note: True, but this option omits the sharp contrast with Amnon's defiling and casting out that so clearly points to Christ.

options.text: By proving that God had abandoned David's house entirely.
options.note: God had not abandoned the covenant; the evil unfolds within His announced discipline, and grace still runs toward Christ.

questions: Amnon called his craving love, but it used Tamar and then despised her. How can you tell the difference between selfish desire and love that seeks another's good?
David was furious but did nothing, leaving Tamar without justice. Where might God be calling you to act, and not merely to feel strongly, on behalf of someone who has been wronged?
Tamar was left desolate, her cry unheard by those who should have defended her. How does it comfort you that God sees and hears the crushed even when people fail them?
Absalom hid his hatred for two years until it erupted in murder. Is there resentment you are nursing in silence, and what would it mean to bring it into the light before it destroys?
This chapter drives us to long for the true Son of David who never casts out those who come to Him. How does Christ's welcome of the wounded and violated shape the way you treat them?

translationNotes.note: Tamar calls the intended act a nebalah, a disgraceful outrage or wicked folly, the grave term the law uses for crimes that violate the covenant community, as in Genesis 34:7.

The BSB footnote notes the 'robe of many colors' can be rendered a long-sleeved robe, the garment worn by the king's virgin daughters, recalling Joseph's robe in Genesis 37:3; Tamar's tearing of it signals her lost status and grief.

The BSB notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint add, after 'he was furious,' the words 'But he would not punish his son Amnon, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn,' explaining David's failure to act; the BSB main text carries the shorter Hebrew reading.
